after: ## Formal and informal control, and sanctions
alt: A two-by-two grid: formal positive sanctions such as awards, formal negative sanctions such as fines and prison, informal positive sanctions such as praise, and informal negative sanctions such as gossip and ostracism. Agencies of each type are listed below.
caption: Cross formal and informal with reward and punishment to generate examples.

alt: Goffman’s three types of stigma (physical differences, perceived flaws of character and tribal stigma) and his distinction between the discredited and the discreditable. Othering, shown by Said and Cohen, legitimises harsher treatment.
caption: Stigma and othering control people by marking them as less than whole.

alt: A grid of six aims of punishment, retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation, reparation and denunciation, each with its meaning and typical forms.
caption: Each aim of punishment implies a different kind of sentence.

alt: Durkheim’s shift from repressive to restitutive law and Foucault’s shift from sovereign to disciplinary power, with a plan of Bentham’s panopticon: cells around a central tower, so inmates never know when they are watched.
caption: Modern control works through surveillance and self-discipline.

alt: Four approaches to crime prevention: community policing, zero-tolerance policing based on broken windows, intelligence-led and predictive policing, and Clarke’s situational crime prevention, with surveillance concepts from Mathiesen and Zuboff.
caption: Policing ranges from building trust to targeting data and design.

alt: Althusser’s repressive state apparatuses (police, courts, prisons, army) and ideological state apparatuses (education, family, religion, media); interpellation as a police officer’s call that a person recognises as addressed to them; and Gramsci’s hegemony through consent.
caption: Force is visible; ideology works when people accept identities as their own.

alt: A grid of functionalist, Marxist, feminist and interactionist views of social control, each with its argument and sociologists such as Durkheim, Hirschi, Althusser, Gramsci, Heidensohn, Becker, Goffman and Cohen.
caption: Consensus views see control protecting everyone; conflict views see it protecting the powerful.
